title: Dance halls gone: New Orleans music scene and Preservation Hall bookings
summary: Few dance halls remain; Tillman describes the thin scene, Bourbon Street clubs, and band leaders who tour out of town.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: I see. Well the, what about the dance halls? You know, I'm not even. Are there any more of them going? No. Dance halls? No.

I'll try, like I say, around this season of the year. There's nothing happening, that's no dance halls. All the crap get a cuff. Every now and then that'll give something, you know. Yeah. Big four. There's a couple of spots. I mean there's nothing much to it. Doudrop, it's a night club, they have about five pieces. They got a couple of other spots with small combos in them, you know. Yeah. This is a great big dead town, that's what it is. As far as the music life, there's no music life. I see. All it's started getting the benefit of this, that's working in the spots around the Boydman Street and the Quarters. And well in True Jeffery he's been getting great smaller contacts with the bands, send them out of town. So every time he send one or two bands out for no while, that's going to hire more horn musicians, which I think is one of the best things you could ever have. I mean to have somebody interested enough to try to keep you doing a little something, you know what I mean? Now you take that Bourbon Street Club, well personally Albert men get straight smaller work out of town, but it don't be for a little time, you see, they don't stay that long. Albert who? Albert French. Oh yeah. Albert French. Yeah they might go off for one or two days and they come right back and the only time outside to get to work in there is when they're gone. The man really would like to have them in there every night. But they work four or five nights I think and they're off by two.
That's Dixieland Hall you're talking about.

Dixieland, yeah. Because Kid Howard they work some off dates but the musicians don't get a chance to work as many off dates in there as they do in Preservation. See, because Jack Fris, in most of those, since he's been playing himself, well quite naturally he's hustling on both angles. And the out of town, the out of town attraction means more to him than staying there. Because if he stay there he don't do nothing but work. So he don't worry about playing at Preservation but when he get on the road, well then he plays.
Oh yeah, I see. So he makes it both ways then. Oh yeah. And then the other people come.

He makes it both ways and they hurt me too. See, because we didn't even play the same instrument. I mean, Charles used to hire me on, he played myself. So that's kind of a hard shift for me but what I'm going to do, he's the boss.
